title: Mandate
pitch: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A bank payment desk where an AI agent can investigate freely but cannot move money without a revocable mandate from a person, built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents are locked out of nearly every high consequence system on earth. Not because they lack the capability, a model can read a payment queue and spot a duplicate or a sanctions hit faster than a person can, but because none of these systems has a way to grant an agent partial authority: enough to be useful, bounded enough to be safe, revocable the instant a human changes their mind. Today the choice is binary. Either the agent gets your credentials and can do everything you can do, or it gets nothing. Every bank, hospital, and factory picks nothing, and rationally so. WebMCP changes where that decision can live. Because tools are defined by the page itself, not by the model or its vendor, the site gets to decide what an agent may do, under what conditions, and for how long. Mandate is what that looks like on a bank's payment operations desk, where getting it wrong moves real money. What it does Mandate is a bank payment operations desk with an AI agent connected through WebMCP. The agent can investigate freely: read the queue, check a beneficiary, ask a partner screening bureau to recheck a sanctions match, but it cannot release a single payment on its own authority. To act, it has to negotiate. It calls propose_mandate , asking for what it needs, for example "up to 5,000 euros a payment, 50,000 total, SEPA only, verified beneficiaries only, for the next thirty minutes." That request shows up on the desk as a card a person can edit before agreeing: tighten the ceiling, shorten the clock, or refuse outright. The moment they grant it, the page re-registers its tool surface and a tool that did not exist a second earlier now does ( release_under_mandate , revoke_mandate ). The moment they revoke it, those tools vanish from the agent's list mid session. Three things fall out of that same property: A refusal is a conversation, not a 403. When the agent tries to release a payment it has no authority for, it gets back a plain English reason ("Segregation of duties: an agent cannot authorise a payment on its own authority") plus the two tools that would actually work, so it reroutes itself. The human sits inside the tool call, not notified after it. request_authorization returns a promise the page only resolves when a person clicks, so the agent is genuinely blocked and comes back with the real human answer. Nothing leaves the tab. All desk state is client side, so a bank could put real positions behind this and the agent would operate on data that never reaches a third party. What people and agents can do together that they could not before Until now an agent on a desk like this had two settings, and both are useless. Read only, in which case a person still makes every keystroke and the agent is a search box. Or the agent holds a human's credentials, in which case it can do everything that human can do and no bank will ever connect it. There was no way to express "you may do this much, for this long, and I can stop you." Three things happen on this desk that had nowhere to live before: An agent asks for authority in its own words, and a person edits the request before granting it. The agent proposes 5,000 euros a payment. Priya makes it 2,500 and grants that instead. The agent is told in its return value that its request was tightened, and works to the smaller number, leaving behind a 3,960 euro payment it would have been allowed to clear under its own proposal. Neither side had to anticipate the other in advance, which is what makes it a negotiation rather than a settings page. Two organisations settle one case without either handing over its data. The desk cannot see the bureau's watchlist. The bureau never sees the desk's payments. The agent asks the desk, the desk brokers the call across origins, and the answer comes back attributed to the bureau with an audit entry on both sides. That used to be a server to server integration with a contract behind it. Here it is one tool published to one named origin, and it works between two independent deployments. Authority ends mid conversation. A person clicks revoke and the tool the agent was about to reach for is gone from getTools() before its next call. Not a rejected request, and not a permission checked inside a handler: the capability itself stops existing while the session is still open. How it creates a better user experience For the person at the desk, the change is that they stop approving things one at a time and start setting a boundary once. Fifteen payments before a cut off used to be fifteen decisions. It becomes one decision about scope, after which the agent clears everything inside that scope and brings back everything outside it with the reason attached: above the ceiling you set, beneficiary not verified, sanctions match, wrong currency for that rail. Nothing is agreed to by accident either, because the ceiling, the budget, the rails, the beneficiary rule and the clock are all on screen and all editable before anyone clicks grant. For the agent, the change is that a refusal stops being a dead end. Every control answers in the shape a colleague would use: what is blocked, why, and what would work instead. So it reroutes itself instead of retrying the same call or inventing a workaround. And the desk keeps a permanent panel showing what the browser is actually holding, read live from getTools() rather than described in prose. Grant a mandate and the count moves from 18 to 20 on screen, in the same frame as the click. Revoke it and it drops back. Being able to see exactly what an agent may do at this moment is the thing you most want to know when you let one near your money, and it is normally the thing you cannot see at all. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP This only works because WebMCP puts tool definitions in the page, computed from live state, instead of behind a static, server hosted tool list. A conventional MCP server hands a fixed set of tools to a client it cannot see. Mandate's tool surface is rebuilt and re-registered against an AbortSignal every time authority changes, so the mandate is real rather than cosmetic: tools do not exist until authority does, and they stop existing the instant it is withdrawn. That loop, an agent asking for authority, a human shaping it, and the tool surface itself changing as a result, is not possible outside a page hosted model. How we built it No backend, no database, no AI model of our own, no build step, and zero runtime dependencies. The visiting agent (Chrome with the WebMCP flag, or ChatGPT's in-app browser) brings the model; the page brings the tools and the governance. Twenty tools across five tiers, plus one published from a separate origin: Read tools with readOnlyHint: true (free rein: search payments, explain a hold, get exposure, pull the audit trail) Prepare tools that move

live_observation.first_impression: A payment-desk UI shows a payment queue, operator selector, authority and audit tabs, cash/rail status headings, and no currently registered agent tools.
live_observation.after_state: The main view changed to Authority and listed connected agent/origin identities, while the agent capability area still reported none registered.
live_observation.notes: The interface makes the human/agent authority boundary visible without requiring login.
